conclusion.justification: The report explicitly states that the claim is not supported by scientific evidence and highlights extensive research demonstrating that childhood vaccines do not cause autism.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
The claim that increasing the number of childhood vaccines causes an increase in autism is not supported by scientific evidence. The concern originated from a 1998 paper that has since been retracted, and subsequent large-scale studies have found no association between vaccines and autism (Johns Hopkins). 

Research shows that the risk of autism is the same in vaccinated and unvaccinated children (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia). A 2014 meta-analysis pooling data from over 1.2 million children found no link between vaccines—including the MMR vaccine and thimerosal-containing vaccines—and the development of autism (Forbes). 

The false impression of a link often arises because autism is typically first identified in children between 12 and 24 months of age, which coincides with the timing of key childhood vaccines (American Academy of Pediatrics). Decades of research involving millions of children consistently demonstrate that neither the number of vaccines nor their ingredients cause autism.

**Sources:**
- https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/vaccines-do-not-cause-autism
- https://www.chop.edu/vaccine-education-center/vaccine-safety/vaccines-and-other-conditions/autism
- https://www.forbes.com/sites/emilywillingham/2014/05/15/vaccines-thimerosal-mmr-mercury-not-associated-with-autism/
- https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/fact-checked/fact-checked-vaccines-safe-and-effect-no-link-to-autism/
